description: A Single Mathematics B-style paper covering vector motion, second-order ODEs, Fourier and Parseval methods, gradients, conservative fields, Jacobians, and statistics.
instructions: Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Answers should be exact unless a numerical approximation is requested.
Begin each main question on a new page when working on paper.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: A particle moves along the space curve \(\mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,3t)\), where \(t\ge0\). Its mass is \(m\).
questions.title: Helical Motion and Force

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed of the particle.
parts.answer: Differentiating the position vector gives \[\mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t)=(-2\sin t,2\cos t,3).\] Differentiating again gives \[\mathbf a(t)=\mathbf r''(t)=(-2\cos t,-2\sin t,0).\] The speed is \[|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+9}=\sqrt{13}.\] Thus the particle has constant speed \(\sqrt{13}\) while moving around a helix of radius \(2\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the curvature of the trajectory and interpret its constancy.
parts.answer: For a space curve, \(\kappa=|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a|/|\mathbf v|^3\). Here \[\mathbf v\times\mathbf a=(6\sin t,-6\cos t,4),\] so \[|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a|=\sqrt{36\sin^2t+36\cos^2t+16}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}.\] Since \(|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{13}\), \[\kappa=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{(\sqrt{13})^3}=\frac{2}{13}.\] The curvature is constant, reflecting that the path bends at the same rate all along the uniform helix.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the force acting on the particle and show that it is perpendicular to the velocity.
parts.answer: Newton's second law gives \[\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=(-2m\cos t,-2m\sin t,0).\] The dot product with velocity is \[\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=(-2m\cos t)(-2\sin t)+(-2m\sin t)(2\cos t)+0=0.\] Hence the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Calculate the work done by this force from \(t=0\) to \(t=2\pi\).
parts.answer: The work is \[W=\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt.\] From part (c), \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=0\) for all \(t\). Therefore \[W=\int_0^{2\pi}0\,dt=0.\] This agrees with the work-energy theorem because the speed, and hence the kinetic energy, is constant.

questions.stem: Answer the following independent questions on second-order linear differential equations.
questions.title: Repeated Roots and Resonance

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The auxiliary equation is \(r^2-4r+4=0\), so \((r-2)^2=0\). The repeated root is \(r=2\), and therefore \[y(t)=(C_1+C_2t)e^{2t}.\] The condition \(y(0)=1\) gives \(C_1=1\). Differentiating, \[y'(t)=e^{2t}\{C_2+2(C_1+C_2t)\}.\] Hence \(y'(0)=C_2+2C_1=3\), so \(C_2=1\). Therefore \[y(t)=(1+t)e^{2t}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Solve \(x''+4x=8\cos 2t\), subject to \(x(0)=0\) and \(x'(0)=0\).
parts.answer: The complementary solution is \(x_c=A\cos2t+B\sin2t\). Since the forcing term \(8\cos2t\) has the same frequency as the complementary solution, use a resonant trial solution \(x_p=Ct\sin2t\). Then \[x_p''+4x_p=4C\cos2t.\] Matching \(8\cos2t\) gives \(C=2\). Thus \[x=A\cos2t+B\sin2t+2t\sin2t.\] The condition \(x(0)=0\) gives \(A=0\). Also \(x'(0)=2B=0\), so \(B=0\). Hence \[x(t)=2t\sin2t.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Briefly explain the physical meaning of the factor \(t\) in the answer to part (b).
parts.answer: The factor \(t\) appears because the applied force oscillates at the natural frequency of the system. In the undamped model this is resonance: energy is added in phase with the motion, so the oscillation amplitude grows linearly with time. The solution \(2t\sin2t\) therefore represents bounded-frequency oscillation with an unbounded envelope.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) for \(-\pi<x<\pi\), extended periodically with period \(2\pi\).
questions.title: Even Fourier Series and Parseval

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the Fourier coefficients of \(f\).
parts.answer: The function is even, so \(b_n=0\) for all \(n\). The constant coefficient is \[a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x^2\,dx=\frac{2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi^3}{3}=\frac{2\pi^2}{3}.\] For \(n\ge1\), \[a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x^2\cos nx\,dx.\] Integrating by parts twice gives \[\int_0^{\pi}x^2\cos nx\,dx=\frac{2\pi(-1)^n}{n^2},\] and hence \[a_n=\frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write the Fourier series and give the first four non-constant terms.
parts.answer: Since \(a_0/2=\pi^2/3\), the Fourier series is \[x^2\sim\frac{\pi^2}{3}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx.\] The first four non-constant terms are therefore \[-4\cos x+\cos2x-\frac{4}{9}\cos3x+\frac14\cos4x.\] The absence of sine terms follows from the even symmetry of \(x^2\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use Parseval's theorem to evaluate \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^4\).
parts.answer: Parseval's theorem gives \[\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^4\,dx=\frac{a_0^2}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n^2.\] The left side is \[\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x^4\,dx=\frac{2\pi^4}{5}.\] Also \(a_0^2/2=2\pi^4/9\) and \(a_n^2=16/n^4\). Therefore \[\frac{2\pi^4}{5}=\frac{2\pi^4}{9}+16\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}.\] Rearranging gives \[16\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}=\frac{8\pi^4}{45},\] so \[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}.\]

questions.stem: The temperature in a laboratory chamber is modelled by \(T(x,y,z)=40+2x^2-y^2+3z\). Distances are measured in metres and temperature in degrees Celsius.
questions.title: Gradient and Directional Derivatives

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(\nabla T\) and evaluate it at \(P=(1,2,-1)\).
parts.answer: The gradient is the vector of first partial derivatives: \[\nabla T=(T_x,T_y,T_z)=(4x,-2y,3).\] At \(P=(1,2,-1)\), this becomes \[\nabla T(P)=(4,-4,3).\] This vector points in the direction of greatest local temperature increase at \(P\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the directional derivative at \(P\) in the direction of the vector \((2,-1,2)\).
parts.answer: First convert the direction vector into a unit vector. Since \(|(2,-1,2)|=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3\), the unit vector is \[\mathbf u=\left(\frac23,-\frac13,\frac23\right).\] The directional derivative is \[D_{\mathbf u}T(P)=\nabla T(P)\cdot\mathbf u=(4,-4,3)\cdot\left(\frac23,-\frac13,\frac23\right).\] Therefore \[D_{\mathbf u}T(P)=\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{3}+2=6.\] The temperature increases at \(6\) degrees Celsius per metre in this direction.

questions.section: Section E: Critical Points and Vector Calculus
questions.stem: Consider the vector field \(\mathbf F(x,y)=(2xy+3, x^2+4y)\) in the plane.
questions.title: Conservative Fields and Line Integrals

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that \(\mathbf F\) is conservative on \(\mathbb R^2\).
parts.answer: Write \(\mathbf F=(P,Q)\), where \(P=2xy+3\) and \(Q=x^2+4y\). For a field on the simply connected plane, equality of the cross partial derivatives is sufficient for conservativeness. Here \[P_y=2x,\qquad Q_x=2x.\] Since \(P_y=Q_x\) everywhere in \(\mathbb R^2\), the field is conservative on \(\mathbb R^2\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find a potential function \(\phi\) such that \(\nabla\phi=\mathbf F\).
parts.answer: We need \(\phi_x=2xy+3\) and \(\phi_y=x^2+4y\). Integrating \(\phi_x\) with respect to \(x\) gives \[\phi(x,y)=x^2y+3x+g(y).\] Differentiating this expression with respect to \(y\) gives \[\phi_y=x^2+g'(y).\] Comparing with \(x^2+4y\), we get \(g'(y)=4y\), so \(g(y)=2y^2+C\). Thus one potential function is \[\phi(x,y)=x^2y+3x+2y^2.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r\), where \(C\) is any smooth path from \((0,1)\) to \((2,3)\).
parts.answer: Because \(\mathbf F\) is conservative, the line integral depends only on the endpoints. Using the potential from part (b), \[\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(2,3)-\phi(0,1).\] Now \[\phi(2,3)=2^2\cdot3+3\cdot2+2\cdot3^2=12+6+18=36,\] while \[\phi(0,1)=0+0+2=2.\] Therefore \[\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=36-2=34.\]

questions.section: Section F: Multiple Integrals and Vector Identities
questions.stem: Let \(R\) be the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\).
questions.title: Changing Order in Double Integrals

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe \(R\) using bounds with \(x\) first and then by switching the order of integration.
parts.answer: The curves meet where \(x^2=2x\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=2\). With vertical slices, \(0\le x\le2\) and \(x^2\le y\le2x\). Thus \[R=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le2x\}.\] To switch the order, note that \(0\le y\le4\). From \(y\le2x\) we get \(x\ge y/2\), and from \(y\ge x^2\) in the first quadrant we get \(x\le\sqrt y\). Hence \[R=\{(x,y):0\le y\le4,\ y/2\le x\le\sqrt y\}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\iint_R y\,dA\) using the switched order from part (a).
parts.answer: Using the switched bounds, \[\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^4\int_{y/2}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx\,dy.\] The inner integral is \[\int_{y/2}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx=y\left(\sqrt y-\frac y2\right)=y^{3/2}-\frac{y^2}{2}.\] Therefore \[\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^4\left(y^{3/2}-\frac{y^2}{2}\right)dy=\left[\frac{2}{5}y^{5/2}-\frac{y^3}{6}\right]_0^4.\] Since \(4^{5/2}=32\), this gives \[\frac{64}{5}-\frac{64}{6}=\frac{32}{15}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the area of \(R\) and hence the \(y\)-coordinate of its centroid.
parts.answer: Using vertical slices, the area is \[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=4-\frac83=\frac43.\] The \(y\)-coordinate of the centroid is \[\bar y=\frac{1}{A}\iint_R y\,dA.\] From part (b), \(\iint_R y\,dA=32/15\), so \[\bar y=\frac{32/15}{4/3}=\frac{32}{15}\cdot\frac34=\frac85.\] Thus the centroid has \(y\)-coordinate \(8/5\).

questions.stem: A detector is tested using independent trials and repeated batch measurements.
questions.title: Binomial, Normal Approximation, and CLT

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: In \(10\) independent tests the detector succeeds with probability \(0.3\) on each test. Find the probability of at least two successes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In a larger run, \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.64)\). Use a normal approximation with continuity correction to estimate \(P(60\le Y\le72)\).
parts.answer: For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.64)\), the mean is \(np=64\) and the variance is \(np(1-p)=100(0.64)(0.36)=23.04\), so the standard deviation is \(4.8\). With a continuity correction, \[P(60\le Y\le72)\approx P(59.5<Y_N<72.5),\] where \(Y_N\sim N(64,4.8^2)\). Standardising gives \[P\left(\frac{59.5-64}{4.8}<Z<\frac{72.5-64}{4.8}\right)=P(-0.94<Z<1.77).\] From normal tables this is approximately \(0.9616-0.1736=0.788\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A batch measurement has mean \(50\) and standard deviation \(12\). For \(36\) independent batches, use the central limit theorem to estimate \(P(\bar X>53)\).
parts.answer: By the central limit theorem, the sample mean \(\bar X\) is approximately normal for \(n=36\), with mean \[E[\bar X]=50\] and standard deviation \[\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=2.\] Therefore \[P(\bar X>53)\approx P\left(Z>\frac{53-50}{2}\right)=P(Z>1.50).\] From standard normal tables, \(P(Z<1.50)\approx0.9332\), so \[P(Z>1.50)\approx1-0.9332=0.0668.\] Thus the required probability is about \(0.067\).
